# Wiring the Application Stack {#sec-wiring-stack}

A production LLM application in 2026 is assembled from parts that most teams
now recognize: clients and an agent runtime, a retrieval service, tools reached
through the Model Context Protocol, a sandbox for code the model writes, a model
gateway in front of hosted and self-hosted models, GPU compute, and
observability with evaluation. The earlier practical chapters treated these one
at a time: models (@sec-choosing-model), serving and compute
(@sec-serving-stack), training (@sec-training-practice), agents and sandboxes
(@sec-agents-practice), retrieval (@sec-retrieval-practice), and evaluation
(@sec-eval-practice). This chapter assembles them into one system, the
application stack; @sec-training-stack assembles the training stack that
produces the models themselves.

The stack is easiest to read as a set of seams, the boundaries where one
component hands a request, a credential, or evidence to another. Most
integration failures happen at a seam: a translation that drops a field, retries
that multiply at every layer, a token that reaches a service it was not issued
for, a trace that cannot show whether an effect happened. The view comes from
systems work that described networks by their constrained interfaces rather
than their products [@fielding2000rest], traced machine-learning debt to glue
code, configuration, and undeclared consumers [@sculley2015debt], and turned
that lesson into production-readiness tests [@breck2017mltest]. The chapter
draws the stack and the paths through it, walks each seam with its tools, its
configuration or code, and its rule, and closes with three reference stacks and
the integration release that makes the stack @sec-whole-stack traced releasable
and reversible.

## The reference architecture

@fig-reference-arch draws the stack by layer. Read from top to bottom, it is the
path of a request. A client calls the runtime; the runtime retrieves evidence,
calls tools through an MCP gateway, runs code in a sandbox, and calls models
through the model @gls-gateway, which forwards each call to a hosted API or to
self-hosted serving on the team's own GPUs. The observability and evaluation
layer at the bottom receives spans from every component and sends its own judge
calls back through the gateway. The color of each arrow is the credential that
the call carries.

```{figure}
//| figure: reference-stack
//| label: fig-reference-arch
//| fig-cap: "A reference stack for an LLM application, by layer, with example projects and products as of September 2026. Arrows are calls, and each arrow's color is the credential the call carries; the dashed bus carries OpenTelemetry GenAI spans, which grant no authority. Selecting a component shows what it does, example choices, and the section of this chapter that covers its seam; with nothing selected, the readout groups the calls by credential. The named projects are examples, not recommendations."
```

Two gateways carry most of the traffic, the model gateway for model calls and
the MCP gateway for tool calls, and the sandbox is the compute seam for code the
model writes. Every path has the same abstract shape: a caller, an admission
decision, an adapter that turns the caller's contract into the provider's, and a
provider. Tool effects take a separately authorized path to an executor that
records each effect, retrieval returns identified evidence, and telemetry
observes every decision without granting any permission.

Three wire formats let the parts compose: HTTP dialects for model calls, MCP for
tool calls, and the OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions for spans. Each is a narrow
interface that lets the implementation behind it change without rewriting its
callers, and each is described with its seam. The traffic divides into three
planes. The data plane carries requests, stream events, evidence, and tool
calls; the control plane applies admission, routing, budgets, authorization,
and overload rules; and the management plane changes routes, credentials,
policies, and releases through a narrower administrative path. One proxy may
serve several planes, but their privileges stay separate. No product sits at the
center, and some fill several boxes: agentgateway and Agent Router carry
both model and MCP traffic, and a hosted sandbox can bundle its own egress
control. The durable part of the figure is the boxes and the credentials on the
arrows.

::: {.callout-note .dated}
## As of September 2026

E2B runs each sandbox in its own Firecracker microVM [@e2b2026runtime], as does
Vercel Sandbox [@vercel2026sandbox], while Modal virtualizes its compute jobs
with gVisor [@modal2026security]. The latest releases of the two open serving
engines named in the figure are vLLM v0.30.0 and SGLang v0.5.20
[@vllm2026repo; @sglang2026serving44]. Two evaluation and observability tools
changed owners this year: ClickHouse acquired Langfuse [@clickhouse2026langfuse],
and Promptfoo announced that it is joining OpenAI through an acquisition
[@promptfoo2026openai].
:::

## Three paths through the stack

The book built the stack along three paths, and the reference architecture is
where they meet.

### From chatbot to agent

A chatbot is one model call. An agent wraps that call in a loop: the model
proposes a tool call, the runtime executes it and returns the result, and the
model chooses the next step (@sec-agent-architectures, @sec-the-harness). Three
additions turn the first into the second, and each is a box in the figure.

- **Grounding through retrieval.** The agent retrieves current, private, or
  authoritative context instead of relying on its weights (@sec-rag-retrieval),
  usually at lower cost than a long context window, whose every token is billed
  on every call (@sec-economics).
- **Actions through tools and a sandbox.** Once the agent runs code, calls an
  API, or writes a file, safety depends on the runtime more than on the model
  (@sec-agents-practice): a jailbreak filter at the gateway does nothing about a
  destructive shell command, and the @gls-sandbox bounds what such a command can
  reach.
- **Durable state through a checkpointer.** A long-running agent keeps its state
  in a checkpointed store so that it survives a restart (@sec-memory-systems).
  LangGraph saves graph state as checkpoints, with a Postgres implementation for
  production [@langgraph2026persistence], and Pydantic AI delegates durable
  execution to workflow engines such as Temporal, DBOS, Prefect, and Restate
  [@pydantic2026durable]. The checkpoint lets a person pause, inspect, and
  resume a task, and lets the framework survive failures in the layers beneath
  it.

### From hosted models to owned ones

The gateway address that fronts a hosted model can also front a model the team
serves itself, or one it fine-tuned (@sec-serving-stack, @sec-training-practice),
so moving from renting capability to owning it changes nothing for callers.
Behind a hosted API, batching, the @gls-kv-cache, speculative decoding, and the
accelerators belong to the provider (@sec-serving-problem) and reach the team as
price terms. When volume and control justify it, the team serves open weights
with vLLM, or with SGLang for traffic that shares long prompt prefixes, and the
per-token cost becomes a GPU bill it schedules; fine-tuning (@sec-sft-peft) adds
a gang-scheduled training run (@sec-orchestration-data-infra). Sustained
utilization decides where a workload sits, and the accounting later in the
chapter computes the break-even share of a month from two prices.

### From usage to evaluation

Every model and tool call is usage that can be observed and scored
(@sec-eval-practice). A leaderboard leader can still misbehave in a product,
because the benchmark measured a generic capability (@sec-benchmarks) while the
product runs its own prompt over its own retrieval context in an agent loop.
Observability records each request's calls with their timing, tokens, and cost;
evaluation scores the traces with deterministic assertions, reference-based
metrics, and a @gls-llm-as-judge, a second model that grades the first against
a calibrated rubric (@sec-judging-holistic). A production trace that fails an
online check joins the regression set that gates the next release
(@sec-evaluating-agents), and failing traces flow back into training data and
agent fixtures.

## The model gateway

A model gateway, also called an LLM gateway or AI gateway, is the control point
between application code and the model providers it calls. In its thinnest form
it is a reverse proxy that accepts one API and forwards to many. Its job is to
hold five concerns in one place: a unified API, custody of provider keys, cost
tracking, routing and fallback, and budgets and policy. Several gateways also
carry tool traffic over MCP and agent-to-agent traffic over A2A.

| Name | What it is | Deployment and license | Fits |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **LiteLLM** | Python SDK and proxy that exposes more than 100 providers in the OpenAI format; virtual keys, budgets, spend tracking, load balancing, admin UI | Self-hosted; MIT outside an enterprise directory, plus a paid enterprise tier | The broadest provider coverage behind one self-hosted proxy |
| **OpenRouter** | Hosted aggregator: one endpoint, prepaid credits, bring-your-own-key | Managed service with a fee on credit purchases | Access to a large model catalog with nothing to operate |
| **Portkey** | Gateway with guardrails, retries and fallbacks, virtual keys, and caching | Open source (MIT), also offered as a hosted service | Guardrails and routing rules kept in the gateway |
| **agentgateway** | Rust proxy that acts as an LLM gateway, an MCP gateway, and an A2A gateway | Self-hosted; Apache 2.0; a Linux Foundation project | One policy point for model, tool, and agent-to-agent traffic |
| **Agent Router** (formerly Envoy AI Gateway) | Gateway on Envoy and Envoy Gateway: model routing, token-based rate limits and quotas, InferencePool support, MCP | Self-hosted on Kubernetes; Apache 2.0; an Agentic AI Foundation project | Platform teams that already run Envoy or the Kubernetes Gateway API |
| **Cloudflare AI Gateway** | Hosted gateway: analytics, logging, caching, rate limiting, retries and fallbacks, unified billing | Managed; core features free | Teams on Cloudflare that want no gateway to operate |
| **Bifrost** (Maxim AI) | Go gateway with one OpenAI-compatible API over more than 20 providers, fallbacks, load balancing, semantic caching | Self-hosted; Apache 2.0, with enterprise features | A self-hosted gateway built with low per-request overhead as a stated goal |

::: {.callout-note .dated}
## As of September 2026

LiteLLM's latest release is v1.102.1 [@litellm2026gateway]. OpenRouter charges
a 5.5 percent fee on credit purchases on its Standard plan and lists more than
500 models from more than 80 providers [@openrouter2026pricing]. Portkey's open
gateway is at v1.15.2 [@portkey2026gateway], and agentgateway at v1.5.0
[@agentgateway2026github44]. Envoy AI Gateway was renamed Agent Router in
September 2026, with the same code, maintainers, and license; its latest release
is v1.1.0 [@agentrouter2026]. Cloudflare's core AI Gateway features are free,
and Unified Billing adds a 5 percent fee on credits [@cloudflare2026aigatewaypricing].
Bifrost's README reports 11 µs of added overhead per request at 5,000 requests
per second, a measurement by its vendor [@bifrost2026maxim44].
:::

Two distinctions matter more than feature lists. A managed gateway (OpenRouter,
Cloudflare AI Gateway, Portkey's hosted service) needs no infrastructure but
passes provider keys and request metadata through a third party; a self-hosted
one (LiteLLM, agentgateway, Agent Router, Bifrost) keeps secrets, logs,
residency, and audit under the team's control. Independently of hosting,
agentgateway and Agent Router put tool and agent traffic under the same policy
point as model calls. Per-request overhead, which vendors measure under their
own conditions, rarely decides a choice, because provider latency exceeds it by
orders of magnitude. What can decide it under agent load is the rate at which
the gateway saturates while it authenticates, meters, applies policy, and
writes spend records, measured with the team's own configuration at its own
peak concurrency.

### Dialects and capability profiles

Model calls travel in three main HTTP dialects: OpenAI Chat Completions
(`/v1/chat/completions`), which open-weight servers such as vLLM and SGLang
expose; OpenAI Responses (`/v1/responses`); and Anthropic Messages
(`/v1/messages`). Coding harnesses have a home dialect: Codex speaks Responses
and Claude Code speaks Messages. A gateway that accepts one dialect and forwards
another translates between them, which is what lets a self-hosted model and a
hosted one share a name, and translation is where meaning is lost: a tool-call
convention, a thinking configuration, a cache hint, a field length.

Similar JSON shapes can carry different semantics. HTTP defines transport
semantics [@rfc9110http] and server-sent events define stream framing
[@whatwg2026sse], but neither defines a provider's tool-call lifecycle, refusal
state, structured-output subset, usage counters, retention, or safety policy.
Each adapter therefore publishes a versioned **capability profile** that puts
every capability in one of four states:

- **native**: the provider implements the declared meaning;
- **adapter-emulated**: the adapter preserves the declared postcondition;
- **lossy**: the adapter changes meaning, and the caller has explicitly accepted
  that downgrade;
- **unsupported**: admission rejects the request before upstream work begins.

The profile covers modalities, endpoint and state model, tool and
parallel-call semantics, the JSON Schema dialect and subset (a provider may
implement only some of the keywords [@jsonschema2020core]), typed stream events,
context and output limits, usage fields, region, retention, and policy. A
translation may preserve, perform an accepted downgrade, or reject; silently
dropping a tool, truncating an identifier, or coercing an unknown field changes
the system without a record. Because the breaks are usually small, a
field-length limit or a request shape that one model generation accepts and the
next rejects, each new pairing of model and harness is smoke-tested with one
tool-bearing request before anything relies on it.

::: {.callout-note .dated}
## As of September 2026

Codex accepts `responses` as the only wire protocol for a model provider
[@openai2026codexconfig]. Claude Code works through a gateway that exposes the
Anthropic Messages format, Bedrock InvokeModel, or Vertex rawPredict and
forwards the `anthropic-version` and `anthropic-beta` headers unchanged
[@anthropic2026gatewayprotocol], and Anthropic does not support routing Claude
Code to non-Claude models through a gateway [@anthropic2026claudecodegateway].
vLLM serves the Anthropic Messages API alongside its OpenAI-compatible API
[@vllm2026repo]. OpenAI's Responses API limits `safety_identifier`, which
replaces the deprecated `user` field, to 64 characters, so a gateway that
receives longer session identifiers from a harness has to hash or shorten them
[@openai2026responsescreate]. Starting with GPT-5.4, Chat Completions does not
support tool calls combined with a reasoning effort other than `none`, so a
gateway that forwards an agent's tool-bearing Chat Completions traffic to a
current reasoning model has to switch it to Responses
[@openai2026migrateresponses]. Anthropic replaced the fixed thinking budget
with adaptive thinking steered by an effort level: Claude 4.7 and later models
reject the budget form with a 400 error, while Claude 4.5 models, including
Haiku 4.5, accept only the budget form [@anthropic2026thinkingtroubleshooting].
A gateway serving both generations therefore needs a capability profile per
model rather than one translation rule. The effort level is guidance, not a
quota: at every level the model decides per request whether to think, and a
request that only processes tool results can skip thinking even at the highest
levels [@anthropic2026steeringthinking].
:::

### Routing, fallback, and keys

The configuration below exposes one alias, `smart`, that fails over from hosted
models to a self-hosted one, so the application never learns which model served
a request. The shape is illustrative rather than any one product's schema:
LiteLLM writes it as a YAML model list, while other gateways bind routing to a
virtual key through an admin API.

```yaml
# Illustrative gateway configuration: one alias, two hosted targets, and a
# self-hosted fallback. Each gateway has its own schema; this is the shape.
models:
  - alias: smart                     # the name the application requests
    target: anthropic/claude-opus-5-5
    api_key: ${ANTHROPIC_API_KEY}    # the provider secret stays in the gateway
  - alias: smart                     # same alias, second provider
    target: openai/gpt-6-sol
    api_key: ${OPENAI_API_KEY}
    upstream_api: responses          # tool calls with reasoning need Responses
  - alias: local                     # self-hosted, behind the same address
    target: vllm/open-weight-model
    base_url: http://vllm.inference.svc:8000/v1

routing:
  smart:
    strategy: fallback               # targets prequalified for one capability profile
    fallback: [local]
    retries: 2                       # the gateway is the single retry owner
# Virtual keys, budgets, and spend caps are issued through the admin API,
# not in this file.
```

Routing applies the capability profiles. The router first filters by hard
constraint (capability, tenant policy, residency, retention, region, and
authority) and then ranks the eligible candidates by measured quality, latency,
availability, or cost. Every accepted operation resolves to an immutable
provider, model revision, adapter revision, capability-profile revision, and
route-policy revision, and canaries use sticky assignment, so repeated work
stays on one system. Fallback changes the system identity: a fallback candidate
must be prequalified inside a declared compatibility class, the candidates whose
capability profiles meet the operation's requirements, under the same policy and
data constraints. The new route is recorded, and after visible output, or after
a side effect whose result is ambiguous, the runtime does not switch systems
silently.

On the caller's side, the seam is an ordinary OpenAI-compatible client. It holds
a **virtual key**, a credential that the gateway issues in place of the provider
secret and scopes to a model allowlist, a budget, and a rate limit, so rotating
a provider secret or capping a runaway agent is a change at the gateway, with no
client redeploy. The OpenAI Python library retries certain errors twice by
default, and `max_retries=0` disables that [@openai2026pythonsdk].

```python
from openai import AsyncOpenAI

llm = AsyncOpenAI(
    base_url="https://llm-gateway.internal/v1",  # the one model address
    api_key=virtual_key,  # scoped gateway key, not a provider secret
    max_retries=0,        # the gateway is the single retry owner
)
```

Nothing in the client names a provider; the gateway resolves the alias,
translates the dialect, and records the route.

### Operations, retries, and overload

The gateway and the runtime treat a request as a **logical operation** that
carries a verified tenant, an `operation_id`, a payload digest, the remaining
deadline, its capability requirements, and the policy revision. Admission
rejects it or records its immutable route, and each upstream call beneath it is
a **physical attempt**, whose frames are normalized into a versioned typed event
stream with operation, attempt, and sequence identifiers. Unknown event types
are surfaced rather than read as text. Refusal, incomplete output, cancellation,
partial output, error, and completion remain distinct terminal outcomes, and a
structured result is validated only after assembly, so a truncation never
passes as a plausible object. Cancellation and the deadline propagate
downstream, and every admitted operation reaches a terminal state through
finite attempts and bounded resources.

Nested client, gateway, adapter, and provider retries create **retry
amplification**. Here $\ell$ denotes a retrying layer and $r_\ell$ its maximum
retry count. The maximum number of physical attempts generated by one logical
operation is

$$
A_{\max}=\prod_{\ell=1}^{L}(1+r_\ell),
$$

where $L$ is the number of independently retrying layers. Two retries at each of
three layers can create $3^3=27$ attempts. The design therefore assigns a single
**retry owner**, the one layer permitted to retry, which is why the client above
sets `max_retries=0` and the configuration sets `retries` at the gateway. The
owner obeys a total attempt limit and the remaining deadline, honors
`Retry-After`, and uses bounded exponential backoff with jitter. Every physical
attempt is recorded, even when the logical operation succeeds. Latency tails in
large fan-out systems are a further reason for these controls [@dean2013tail].
@fig-wiring-retry-amplification shows how much of that bound a failing provider
receives.

```{figure}
//| figure: retry-amplification
//| label: fig-wiring-retry-amplification
//| fig-cap: "Physical attempts generated by one logical operation when $L$ layers each retry up to $r$ times, against a single retry owner. The tree outlines every call each layer can issue, with $A_{\max}$ physical attempts in the bottom row ($\prod_\ell (1 + r_\ell)$ when every layer retries, $1 + r$ with one owner), and fills the calls made in one seeded run at the chosen failure probability $p$. The chart gives the expected physical attempts per logical operation, $(1 - p^{A_{\max}})/(1 - p)$, with attempts failing independently: as $p$ approaches 1, when the provider is already failing, nested retries send up to $A_{\max}$ times the offered load. Under real overload the failure rate rises with that load, which is how a retry storm forms; backoff, deadlines, and `Retry-After` are not modeled."
```

The retry owner decides from a stable error envelope, never from prose. Errors
travel as RFC 9457 problem details [@rfc9457problem], with media type
`application/problem+json`, carrying a stable problem type, a safe upstream
error category, HTTP status, provider code, upstream request ID, operation ID,
attempt number, whether output was partial, whether the operation is retryable,
and any `Retry-After` value; the original cause stays in protected diagnostics.
Authentication, authorization, invalid input, unsupported capability, policy
refusal, and exhausted quota are normally not retryable. Overload and transient
transport failures may be retried only within the operation's budget and
deadline, and never after the caller has seen output, because a replay can
duplicate or contradict the stream.

An idempotency key is an application-level contract, because HTTP by itself does
not deliver a request exactly once. The key is bound to tenant, route class,
operation key, canonical payload digest, and time to live; reusing it with a
different payload is an error, and where the provider cannot deduplicate, the
contract states that exactly-once is not guaranteed. Overload controls are
bounded too: per-tenant concurrency, queue length, stream buffer, tokens, and
tool fan-out. A bounded queue exposes backpressure instead of hidden memory
growth, excess work is shed with `429` or `503` and a `Retry-After` value, and
circuit breakers and retry budgets keep recovery traffic from becoming a retry
storm.

## The tool seam

Tool traffic converged further than model traffic did. The @gls-mcp
standardizes host, client, and server messages over JSON-RPC, with capability
negotiation, discovery, and tool schemas [@mcp2026spec44], so one tool server
serves every agent host (@sec-agents-practice). In production, agents reach tool
servers through an MCP gateway that holds their credentials, applies the
reviewed catalog as an allowlist, meters calls, and writes the audit trail.
Because MCP is a wire protocol, moving a tool from an in-process server to a
remote one behind the gateway changes the connection, not the agent code.

::: {.callout-note .dated}
## As of September 2026

The current MCP revision, 2026-07-28, makes the protocol stateless: it removes
the initialization handshake and protocol-level sessions, and every request
carries its own protocol version and client capabilities [@mcp2026release].
Version 2 of the MCP Python SDK, the current stable line, supports that
revision; its `Client` connects over Streamable HTTP when given a URL, and
headers and authentication go on the `httpx2` client passed to
`streamable_http_client` [@mcp2026pythonsdk].
:::

The code below completes the client above with one agent task. It reaches
tools through the MCP gateway over Streamable HTTP with a tool token whose
audience is the MCP gateway, a credential separate from the virtual key.

```python
import json

import httpx2
from mcp import Client
from mcp.client.streamable_http import streamable_http_client

async def answer(question: str) -> str:
    async with httpx2.AsyncClient(
        headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {tool_token}"},  # audience: the MCP gateway
        timeout=httpx2.Timeout(30.0, read=300.0),
    ) as http:
        transport = streamable_http_client("https://mcp-gateway.internal/mcp", http_client=http)
        async with Client(transport) as tools:
            listed = await tools.list_tools()  # the allowlisted catalog for this token
            schema = [{"type": "function", "function": {"name": t.name,
                       "description": t.description, "parameters": t.input_schema}}
                      for t in listed.tools]
            messages = [{"role": "user", "content": question}]
            for _ in range(8):  # a bounded loop
                reply = await llm.chat.completions.create(
                    model="smart", messages=messages, tools=schema)
                message = reply.choices[0].message
                if not message.tool_calls:
                    return message.content
                messages.append(message)
                for call in message.tool_calls:
                    result = await tools.call_tool(
                        call.function.name, json.loads(call.function.arguments))
                    text = "\n".join(b.text for b in result.content if b.type == "text")
                    messages.append({"role": "tool", "tool_call_id": call.id, "content": text})
            raise RuntimeError("step limit reached without an answer")
```

The client speaks Chat Completions to the gateway, which forwards `smart` in
the dialect each target requires. Tool arguments are parsed only from a
complete message, so partial arguments never execute; a streaming runtime
accumulates fragments and parses them once the tool block ends. A failing tool
returns a result with `is_error` set rather than raising, so the model reads the
failure. The loop itself authorizes nothing. Discovering a tool grants no
authority to call it, and a tool annotation is untrusted metadata. The
integration pins the MCP revision, transport, and negotiated capabilities, and
the MCP gateway and the tool executor behind it authorize each invocation under
the controls in @sec-security-authorization:

1. Authenticate user and workload; derive the tenant from verified identity.
2. Validate the tool name against the allowlist and canonicalize the complete
   arguments against pinned input and output schemas.
3. Classify the effect as read, reversible write, or irreversible/external.
4. Authorize the principal, workload, tenant, tool revision, resource, audience,
   canonical arguments, effect class, and policy revision; bind expiring consent
   or approval where required.
5. Append an intent record, broker a least-privilege credential, and execute with
   an effect-level idempotency key.
6. Persist an effect receipt before advancing the workflow checkpoint; validate
   and redact the result before returning it.

A model-request idempotency key cannot make a tool idempotent, so the effect
carries its own. After an ambiguous timeout, the runtime queries the receipt or
the target state instead of retrying a non-idempotent effect, and canceling a
call leaves any effect that already happened in place. Parallel calls carry
independent call IDs and receipts, and each result keeps its originating call ID
so it cannot attach to the wrong proposal.

The sandbox is the compute side of the same seam. A @gls-sandbox reduces blast
radius, the damage an inappropriate action can do, while authorization decides
whether the action is appropriate. Its threat model bounds filesystem,
syscalls, processes, CPU, memory, disk, wall-clock time, workspace lifetime, and
network. It enforces egress and resource allowlists and validates DNS and every
redirect hop, blocking private, link-local, and metadata endpoints. Secrets stay
outside: code inside receives a short-lived scoped token, or a placeholder that
the egress proxy replaces with the real secret on the way to an allowlisted
host.

## Retrieval and evidence

The retrieval seam returns evidence rather than text. Its common pipeline is
@gls-hybrid-search: lexical BM25 scores and dense-vector similarity are merged
by reciprocal rank fusion, which scores each document by adding
$1/(k + \text{rank})$ over the ranked lists, with $k$ a small smoothing
constant, and a reranker, a model that rescores a short candidate list against
the query, orders the result (@sec-retrieval-practice). The embedding and rerank
models are called through the model gateway, so they are keyed and budgeted
like any model call, and the agent usually reaches retrieval as a tool through
the MCP gateway.

Retrieval is authorized before candidate documents cross the retrieval
service's boundary, because no prompt can make safe a document the caller was
not allowed to read. Every result carries an evidence ID, source and corpus
revision, index revision, authorization decision, and tenant boundary, so an
answer can cite what it used and an evaluation can reproduce it. Cache,
checkpoint, session, task, and deduplication keys include tenant and
system-policy identity, so no stored result crosses a tenant boundary.

## Identity and credentials

A gateway credential, a workload identity, a delegated user token, and a
provider secret answer different questions: which budget a call spends, which
service calls, on whose behalf, and with what authority at the provider. No
application, agent, evaluation harness, or sandbox holds a raw provider
credential. Each holds a virtual key for model traffic and a separately scoped
token for tools, so keys stay separate from effects: a leaked virtual key can
spend a budget but cannot call a tool.

Short-lived workload identity and OAuth token exchange [@rfc8693tokenexchange]
bind every other token to an audience, scope, verified tenant, subject or
actor, and time to live. Each resource server validates its own audience, and a
token issued for one resource is never passed to another. A provider that
supports only a static secret gets a broker that substitutes the secret at an
allowed egress boundary, which is why the provider-secret color in
@fig-reference-arch appears only on the gateway's calls to providers and the
egress proxy's calls out. Zero-trust guidance likewise treats network location
as insufficient authority [@nist2020zerotrust], and management-plane
credentials never travel on the data plane.

## Telemetry as evidence

Telemetry converged on the OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions, a
vendor-neutral set of `gen_ai.*` span attributes for model calls, retrieval, and
agent steps (@sec-eval-practice), so a component instrumented once can send the
same spans to Langfuse, Phoenix, or a general tracing backend. W3C Trace Context
supplies correlation identifiers across services [@w3c2021tracecontext], and
they carry no authority: principal, tenant, and permission are never inferred
from `traceparent` or from baggage, the key-value context that travels with a
trace. Baggage has no built-in integrity, carries no secret, personal data, or
authorization decision, and is allowlisted and stripped at each trust boundary.

::: {.callout-note .dated}
## As of September 2026

The GenAI conventions now live in their own repository and are still marked as
in development, with no tagged release, so an integration pins the convention
version it emits [@otel2026genaisemconv].
:::

The trace records the operation and attempt IDs, route and adapter revisions,
capability decision, error category, tool intent and receipt, evidence IDs, and
terminal outcome. Missing telemetry, exporter loss, sampling, and redaction
failure are reported too, because a trace is partial evidence and cannot by
itself show whether an effect occurred. Evaluation uses the same seams: the
harness and the judge call models through the gateway, so an A/B comparison of
two models is a routing rule. A Promptfoo configuration points its provider's
`apiBaseUrl` at the gateway and names the harness's own key with `apiKeyEnvar`
[@promptfoo2026openaiprovider], and the judge is a model from a different family
on a separately budgeted key.

### The accepted task

The unit of accounting is the whole accepted task, a task whose result passed
acceptance, rather than a model-call subtotal. Cost includes every physical
attempt, model usage, retrieval, tool execution, any judge model that grades the
result, infrastructure, and human review. Latency is the elapsed time of the
root operation; parallel child durations are not summed. Prices use the exact
response model, region, billing time, currency, and price-catalog revision
rather than a mutable alias (@sec-economics, @sec-serving-problem). For task
$q$, a useful accounting identity is

$$
C_q=\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}_q}\sum_{m\in\mathcal{M}_a}u_{a,m}p_m(v_a,\rho_a,t_a,k_a)
    +C_{\mathrm{infra}}+C_{\mathrm{human}},
$$

where $\mathcal{A}_q$ is the set of physical attempts, $\mathcal{M}_a$ contains
disjoint billing meters for attempt $a$, $u_{a,m}$ is usage on meter $m$, and
$p_m$ is its price for response-model revision $v_a$, region $\rho_a$, billing
time $t_a$, and price-catalog revision $k_a$. The remaining terms cover shared
infrastructure and human review. Disjoint meters prevent cached or reasoning
subtotals from being counted twice.

Build-versus-rent is settled by a measured crossover point that differs from
one contract to the next. The two prices in the chart are editable placeholders
that carry no recommendation; a real comparison uses current contract quotes.

```{figure}
//| figure: reserved-breakeven
//| label: fig-wiring-a-2026-stack-cost-crossover
//| fig-cap: "Monthly cost against GPU-hours used in a 720-hour month, with the chapter's placeholder prices, which the controls edit. Serverless billing rises with each used hour, $r \cdot h$; the reserved bill $F$ is flat, so the two break even at $h^* = F/r$, which the top axis reads as a share of the month, the fraction the runnable below computes. The bars split the reserved bill between the hours used and the hours left idle at the chosen use. When $F/r$ exceeds 720 hours, the reserved bill costs more at any use within the month. A decision replaces both prices with current quotes and also counts operations and reliability costs, which the figure leaves out."
```

:::: {.runnable}
```python
def crossover_utilization(serverless_rate, reserved_monthly, hours=720):
    """Return the utilization fraction where pay-per-use equals the flat bill."""
    if serverless_rate <= 0 or reserved_monthly < 0 or hours <= 0:
        raise ValueError("rates and hours must define a non-negative comparison")
    return reserved_monthly / (serverless_rate * hours)

example = crossover_utilization(4.0, 1440.0)
assert abs(example - 0.5) < 1e-12
print(f"illustrative crossover = {example:.0%}")
```
::::

@sec-scaling-laws and @sec-accelerators-networking explain why workload shape,
memory, batching, and hardware efficiency matter beyond the simple curve.

## Three reference stacks

No single stack fits every team, but three archetypes cover most of them. The
rows are the layers of @fig-reference-arch; a team picks the column that
matches its constraints and reads down it. The entries are examples as of
September 2026 and starting points to adapt, not rankings.

| Layer | Lean, managed | Regulated, self-hosted | Cloud-native Kubernetes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Model** | Hosted frontier APIs (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google) with pinned model IDs | Hosted models for hard steps, self-hosted open weights for bulk traffic | The same, with open-weight models served in the cluster |
| **Gateway** | OpenRouter or Cloudflare AI Gateway | LiteLLM, agentgateway, or Bifrost, self-hosted, with virtual keys and budgets | Agent Router or agentgateway in the cluster |
| **Serving** | None operated; the API is the server | vLLM behind an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, with FP8 weights and prefix caching | vLLM or SGLang, with llm-d or NVIDIA Dynamo for cache-aware routing at scale |
| **Agent runtime** | OpenAI Agents SDK or Claude Agent SDK | LangGraph with a checkpointer, or Pydantic AI with durable execution | LangGraph with a Postgres checkpointer |
| **Sandbox** | E2B or Vercel Sandbox, hosted microVMs | Self-hosted Firecracker or gVisor with default-deny egress | Sandboxes in the same cluster under gVisor, with scoped tokens |
| **Retrieval** | A managed search service (turbopuffer, Pinecone) with Cohere Embed and Rerank | Postgres with pgvector and pgvectorscale, open embeddings such as BGE-M3 | Qdrant with hybrid queries and an open reranker |
| **Evaluation and observability** | LangSmith or Braintrust, hosted | Self-hosted Langfuse, with Promptfoo or DeepEval in CI | Phoenix or another OpenTelemetry backend, with DeepEval in CI |
| **Compute** | GPUs billed by use (Modal, Baseten, Fireworks, Together) | Committed capacity from a neocloud (CoreWeave, Lambda), with Slurm and Kubernetes | Kubernetes with Kueue quotas and Volcano or KAI Scheduler gang scheduling |

::: {.callout-note .dated}
## As of September 2026

Cohere's current retrieval models are `embed-v4.0` and the `rerank-v4.0-pro`
and `rerank-v4.0-fast` rerankers [@cohere2026models]. Qdrant fuses dense and
sparse results in a single hybrid query and describes reciprocal rank fusion as
the safe default [@qdrant2026hybrid]. Modal bills GPUs per second of use,
listing an NVIDIA H100 at $0.001097 per second [@modal2026pricing44].
:::

The advice under the table outlasts its entries. Keep new moving parts few.
Spend the quality budget on retrieval and reranking before a more elaborate
vector database, and on calibrated judges before more benchmarks. Keep every
layer behind the shared wire formats and hard-code no vendor, because the
archetype a team starts in is rarely the one it ends in.

## The integration release

Connected products become one releasable system when every boundary has a
contract, every component that affects behavior has an identity, and a failed
release has a tested way back. The unit that carries all three is the
**integration release**, a versioned statement of what is connected, what each
connection means, who owns it, and what evidence makes the assembly safe to
release. It starts from the release decision: the capability, its users and
tenants, its permitted data classes and effects, its quality and operational
thresholds, and its rollback trigger. It then freezes a **system fingerprint**
of the model, prompt, retrieval snapshot, tool schema, policy, router
configuration, telemetry schema, and artifact digests, because a model name
alone cannot identify the system that produced an answer.

The release owns two kinds of record: the **system manifest**, which
identifies the assembled system, and the **boundary contracts**, which collect
the rules the seams above state for each producer and consumer. Neither may
contain a mutable alias such as `latest`.

| Record | Required fields | Release question |
| --- | --- | --- |
| System manifest | application, model, prompt, retrieval, tool, policy, router, telemetry, and artifact revisions | Can this exact behavior be identified again? |
| Topology | every producer, consumer, protocol version, transport, and owner | Does every live edge have an accountable owner? |
| Capability profile | native, adapter-emulated, lossy, or unsupported behavior | What meaning changes at an adapter? |
| Trust contract | principal, workload, tenant, authority, audience, scope, and data class | May this caller send this data or cause this effect? |
| Failure contract | deadline, cancellation, retry owner, idempotency scope, error mapping, and backpressure | Where does failure stop, and who may retry? |
| Evidence contract | telemetry, conformance result, migration state, acceptance evidence, and rollback revision | What proves the release and restores the last good one? |

The manifest is signed or otherwise integrity-protected and records a software
bill of materials, build provenance, artifact digests, schema revisions, policy
bundles, and the exact route table. in-toto models verifiable supply-chain steps
[@torresarias2019intoto], and SLSA defines progressively stronger provenance
requirements [@slsa2026spec]. These controls distinguish the tested artifact
from a later substitution; whether it behaves correctly is still for the tests
to establish.

### Boundary tests

Every adapter and boundary passes the same conformance fixtures before it joins
a release.

| Fixture | Required assertion |
| --- | --- |
| Unary request | exact request identity, terminal status, usage, and error mapping |
| Stream interruption | ordered typed events, partial status, no replay after visible output |
| Tool arguments | no execution before complete parse, schema validation, authorization, and call-ID binding |
| Structured output | final local validation; refusal, incomplete, and schema error remain distinct |
| Rate limit and overload | `Retry-After`, bounded queue behavior, cancellation, and correct `429` or `503` |
| Retry and fallback | one retry owner, finite attempts, compatible fallback, and changed system identity |
| Tenant isolation | wrong-audience token, cross-tenant cache or handle, stale approval, and secret leakage all fail closed |
| Telemetry | operation/attempt correlation, route decision, missing telemetry, and redaction are visible |

Negative fixtures cover unknown stream events, duplicate delivery, a worker
crash after commit but before receipt, malicious tool output, schema drift, DNS
rebinding, redirect to a metadata endpoint, filesystem escape, and runaway
process creation. A successful demo exercises none of these paths.

### Cutover and rollback

Migration is itself an integration, and the cutover runs in a fixed order:
adapter contract tests; a shadow of new read-only behavior with no side effects;
a sticky canary that keeps each task or tenant on one fingerprint; and a ramp
that proceeds only while quality, security, latency, error, and cost gates hold.
Route and policy changes are published atomically, the last-known-good manifest
stays deployable, and rollback is tested before the first canary receives
traffic.

```{dot}
//| label: fig-cutover-path
//| fig-cap: "A reversible integration cutover. Contract tests precede a side-effect-free shadow, sticky canary, staged ramp, and release. Any failed gate restores the last-known-good manifest."
digraph {
  bgcolor="transparent"; rankdir=TB; nodesep=0.16; ranksep=0.24;
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=9,
        color="#6b7280", fontcolor="#6b7280", fillcolor="#f1ece1"];
  edge [fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=9, color="#6b7280", arrowsize=0.65];
  tests [label="Contract tests"];
  shadow [label="Shadow"];
  canary [label="Sticky canary"];
  ramp [label="Staged ramp"];
  release [label="Release"];
  lkg [label="Last-known-good"];
  tests -> shadow -> canary -> ramp -> release;
  shadow -> lkg [label="fail"];
  canary -> lkg [label="fail"];
  ramp -> lkg [label="fail"];
}
```

Each failure has a detection signal and an owned containment and recovery
action.

| Failure | Detection | Containment and recovery |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Silent capability loss | capability and conformance mismatch | reject admission; restore prior adapter |
| Retry storm | attempt amplification and queue alarms | disable nested retries; shed load |
| Credential leak | secret canary or audience violation | revoke, rotate, and quarantine evidence |
| Cross-tenant access | authorization and isolation fixture | fail closed; invalidate affected caches and handles |
| Partial tool execution | intent without a matching effect receipt | query target state; reconcile rather than replay |
| Configuration drift | signed-manifest or digest mismatch | stop rollout; restore atomic last-known-good state |
| Missing telemetry | export and coverage SLO breach | halt evidence-dependent release decisions |

From release decision to ramp, the lifecycle is short enough to rehearse. Its
output is an integration release record: the exact manifest, boundary
contracts, test evidence, accepted degradations, rollout state, known gaps,
owners, expiry, and rollback procedure, which @sec-deployment-lifecycle takes as
its input.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Constraint arrow
The gateway is where a lower layer's economics reach the whole application:
because every model call passes one address, the per-token price of a hosted
frontier model (@sec-economics) and the cost of self-hosted serving
(@sec-serving-problem) become routing rules that every caller inherits. Meaning
flows the same way. Provider limits constrain adapters, adapters constrain
routing, routing and authorization constrain the application, and the
fingerprint constrains what an evaluation can claim. An upper layer cannot
recover semantics that a lower boundary silently removed, so the lowest
boundary that knows about a loss has to make it visible.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## What's contested
Some teams expose one provider-shaped API everywhere; others keep provider-native
clients behind a narrower domain interface. Some centralize admission in one
gateway that also carries tool and agent-to-agent traffic; others keep model,
tool, and agent traffic on separate proxies, so that a fault or a compromise in
one does not reach the others. Either can work, and each topology has to meet
the same requirements: explicit semantic loss, least authority, bounded
failure, immutable identity, end-to-end evidence, and tested rollback. The
reference stack in this chapter is a snapshot of named products; the seams and
their contracts are the part expected to outlast it.
:::
